A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same UBA learning-rate scheduling work and contain 43 pages, including Appendices A–F. Text extraction and visual inspection support comparison of the text, equations, tables and figures without material gaps.

before.justification: v1 reports original vision-classification and OLMo training experiments, numerical fitting results and ablations in Section 4 and Appendices B and E.

after.justification: v3 retains the original numerical fitting, vision-classification, OLMo and ablation results, including accuracy measurements and training curves.

M1.justification: The min-max framework, projected-gradient and curve-fitting construction, UBA formula in equation (5), parameter φ and single-phase/multi-phase procedures remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same CIFAR10, CIFAR100 and ImageNet classification tasks and OLMo language benchmarks documented in Appendix E. No dataset, domain or test scenario is added or removed.

E2.justification: SS, CS, CLR, 1C, BT and REX remain the evaluated baselines. The OLMo-300M comparison still uses CS, BT and REX in Table 8. Newly discussed related-work methods are not added to the experiments.

E3.justification: Section 4 and Appendix E retain the same data splits, epoch and token budgets, model configurations, optimizer settings, warmup procedures and evaluation metrics.

E4.justification: The numerical-fitting checks, cross-optimizer comparison, φ sensitivity study and phase-count analysis remain unchanged, including Appendix B and Appendices E.6–E.8, Tables 9–11 and Figure 11.

E5.justification: Appendix B and Figure 5 retain the same standard-deviation visualization for the fitted parameter relationship. Neither version reports training seeds, repeated-training-run counts or significance tests.

E6.justification: The numerical tables and plotted results are unchanged, including UBA's 79.32% ImageNet accuracy at 300 epochs and 50.42% average accuracy for OLMo-300M. Appendix fitting results and ablation entries also match.

T1.justification: The finite-optimization definition, equations (1)–(8), Propositions 1–2, Theorem 1 and derivations and proofs in Appendices A–D are retained. Differences are citation renumbering and typesetting, not revised mathematical content.

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list and conclusion retain the same claims about theoretical grounding, single-parameter schedule unification, convergence and performance across architectures, tasks and training budgets.

C2.justification: The interpretations connecting φ to optimization difficulty and AdamW preconditioning remain unchanged. Both versions retain the limitations concerning quantifying optimization difficulty and selecting phase-specific φ values.

D1.justification: The numerical-fitting instructions and Appendix E implementation disclosures retain the same hyperparameters, software, hardware, OLMo configurations and UBA code-access statement. No reproducibility information is added or removed.

R1.justification: v3 adds Zhang et al.'s finite-horizon optimization and Defazio et al.'s optimal linear-decay scheduling work. Section 2 and Appendix F also explicitly describe the already-cited Eigencurve, separating it from elastic step decay. These are limited additions and refinements to research positioning.

P1.justification: v3 removes duplicated introductory wording, makes small grammatical corrections, expands related-work prose and clarifies references to Figure 11 and Appendix E.8. The section sequence and overall narrative remain intact.

P2.justification: Figure 1 moves from page 5 to page 6, and main-text equations, tables and paragraphs reflow; the conclusion is consolidated on page 10. The figure contents and table structures remain unchanged, with no displays added or removed.

improvement.justification: v3 provides more complete scholarly context by acknowledging finite-horizon optimization and theoretical scheduling research, while clarifying Eigencurve's distinct contribution. Small wording and navigation corrections also improve readability. These are limited gains because the method, theoretical arguments, empirical evidence and reproducibility information remain unchanged.
